Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$3\sqrt{3},$ as shown above. Find the greatest possible perimeter ${P}_{\text{max}}$ of the triangle. Do not round the answer.

${P}_{\text{max}}=$
 {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
P(l)=6\sqrt{3}+l+\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $6\sqrt{3},$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<6\sqrt{3}.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{(-2l)}{\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{108-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =108-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =108 \\ {l}^{2} & =54 \\ l & =3\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=3\sqrt{6}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,3\sqrt{6})$ | $3\sqrt{6}$ | $(3\sqrt{6},6\sqrt{3})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ | $$ | $9$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=3\sqrt{6}$ gives the maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter ${P}_{\text{max}}$ that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{\text{max}}=P(3\sqrt{6}) & =6\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{108-54} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{54} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}+6\sqrt{6} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
